988.title: Philip and James (3 May)
988.hook: Philip asks show us the Father, and James leads the church of Jerusalem
988.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saints Philip and James as one feast on 3 May, with readings that often include Philip's request in John 14; the apostles are honored together in the Mass of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph the Worker, the carpenter at his bench on the first of May. Your line was work is holy. Which dull task did you do slowly and well? Day nine hundred eighty-eight.

It's the last night before the cross. Jesus has washed their feet and is talking about leaving. He says they know the way to where he's going. Thomas has already said, honestly, that they don't. Then Philip speaks up. He doesn't ask for a miracle or a seat in the kingdom. He asks for one thing, and adds that it would be enough. Two apostles share a feast on the third of May, and one of them is remembered for asking to see God. Today, Philip and James.
screen: `THE LAST NIGHT.` → `THOMAS: WE DON'T KNOW THE WAY.` → `PHILIP HAS ONE REQUEST.`

segments.voice: Here is Philip's request in the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, shew us the Father, and it is enough for us." It's a hungry question. Just let us see God, once, and we'll ask for nothing else. And Jesus answers with a question of his own. Have I been with you so long, Philip, and you haven't known me? Then: "Philip, he that seeth me seeth the Father also." Catholics hear in that line one of the deep claims of their faith: that in Jesus, God has a face. On that reading, there is no climbing past him to reach the Father, and Philip had been looking at the answer for years. The other apostle today is James, whom Mark's Gospel calls James the less. The Latin tradition identifies him with James, son of Alphaeus, from the lists of the twelve, and also with the James whom Paul calls the brother of the Lord, the one who speaks with authority at the council in Jerusalem in Acts. Scholars and churches don't all agree that these are one man, and the Gospels don't settle it. What the Church does with the two of them is pair them on one day, and the pairing works. Philip asks to see. James, in the tradition, stays, and serves the church in Jerusalem, in the city where it all happened. One asks the question. The other, tradition says, spends his life in the city where, for Catholics, the answer stood. Some Catholics pray Philip's line as it is, a whole prayer in a sentence.
screen: `PHILIP: SHOW US THE FATHER.` · `WHO SEES ME SEES THE FATHER.` · `WHICH JAMES? TRADITION SAYS ONE MAN.` · `ONE ASKS; ONE STAYS AND SERVES.` · then, large: `LORD, SHEW US THE FATHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask to be shown. Settle, and breathe. Let your shoulders drop. Philip didn't dress his question up, so don't dress yours up either. If you pray, you can say his line slowly, Lord, show us the Father, and then stop talking and wait. If you don't pray, ask the plainest version of your own biggest question, the one you rarely say aloud, and then sit with it open, without rushing to answer it. Notice what is already in front of you. The bell holds the time.
Philip, one of two apostles sharing this feast with James. He asked to see the Father, and James, tradition remembers, led the church in Jerusalem.
Your line: show us the father. Today, ask one honest question out loud, to God or to a friend, instead of pretending you already know. Day nine hundred eighty-eight.

989.title: Matthias (14 May)
989.hook: the apostle chosen by lot to replace Judas
989.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Matthias on 14 May, reading the account of his choosing from Acts 1 at Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Philip and James, the apostle who asked to see God and the one remembered in Jerusalem. Your line was show us the father. What honest question did you ask out loud? Day nine hundred eighty-nine.

An upper room in Jerusalem, after the ascension. The apostles are waiting, praying, and there is an empty place among them. Judas is gone. Peter stands up and says the place has to be filled. Not by anyone. By someone who has walked with them the whole way, from John's baptism to the day Jesus was taken up. Two names are put forward. Then, instead of a vote or a speech, they do something that may sound strange. Today, the man who got the empty seat. Matthias.
screen: `AN EMPTY PLACE.` → `PETER: IT MUST BE FILLED.` → `TWO NAMES.`

segments.voice: Here's how Acts tells it. The two men are Joseph called Barsabas, also named Justus, and Matthias. The apostles pray, asking the Lord, who knows every heart, to show which one he has chosen. Then they cast lots. In the Douay-Rheims: "And they gave them lots, and the lot fell upon Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles." That's it. The lot falls. He's in. Three things stand out. First, the qualification. Matthias wasn't new. He'd been there all along, through the roads and the crowds and the cross, without ever being named. He was a witness before he was an apostle. Second, the lot. Acts presents the lot as a way of leaving the choice to God: they prayed first, then let the answer fall. Some readers notice that after the Spirit comes at Pentecost, a few verses later, Acts never shows the apostles choosing this way again. Third, the silence. After this verse, Acts doesn't mention Matthias again. Tradition tells stories of where he preached, but the text gives him one moment. And it's not an easy moment. He is the man who takes the place of a betrayer. Every time someone counts the twelve, there he is, filling a gap left by grief and scandal. Catholics honor him as a full apostle anyway. Not a substitute. Not second best. The one the lot fell on, who had been quietly faithful long before anyone wrote his name down.
screen: `TWO NAMES, A PRAYER, A LOT.` · `A WITNESS BEFORE AN APOSTLE.` · `ONE VERSE, THEN SILENCE.` · `HE FILLS A PLACE LEFT BY BETRAYAL.` · then, large: `THE LOT FELL UPON MATTHIAS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say yes to the role you didn't pick. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a place you've ended up that you didn't choose. Covering for someone who left. Caring for a parent. A job that fell to you because nobody else would take it. Notice how it feels to stand in someone else's spot. Then notice what you'd been doing before, quietly, that made you ready for it. If you pray, you can offer that role to God as it is. If you don't, simply let yourself accept it for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Matthias. The disciple who had walked with Jesus all along, chosen by lot to fill the place left by Judas.
Your line: the replacement. Today, if you're covering for someone, do it as if the place were yours, not as a stand-in counting the days. Day nine hundred eighty-nine.

what a scholar hears: Acts 1:21–26 sets the rule, from John's baptism to the ascension; the lot is cast before Pentecost, and Acts names Matthias nowhere else.

990.title: Isidore the Farmer (15 May)
990.hook: a Spanish farmworker whose ploughing, legend says, angels helped with while he prayed
990.howItsDone: Catholics in farming areas often keep Saint Isidore's day on 15 May with Masses and blessings of fields, animals or tractors, and pray for farmers and a good harvest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Matthias, the faithful disciple the lot fell on. Your line was the replacement. Whose place did you fill, or who filled yours? Day nine hundred ninety.

What does a landowner do when his workers complain about one of their own? This one, near Madrid, rides out early in the morning to check on his hired man. The hired man, they say, comes late to the fields every day. He stops at church first. So the landowner goes to see for himself. And here the story turns into legend. Out in the field, the hired man's plow is moving. Beside it, another plow, pulled by white oxen, driven by figures nobody can name. Today, a saint who never left the farm. Isidore the Farmer.
screen: `THE OTHER WORKERS COMPLAIN.` → `THE LANDOWNER RIDES OUT.` → `A SECOND PLOW IN THE FIELD.`

segments.voice: Isidore worked land that belonged to someone else. Tradition says he married a woman named Maria, who is honored too, and that the two of them lived simply and shared what little they had. That's close to all the story needs. He left no writings and held no office. He plowed. The legend of the angels is told in more than one version, and it isn't in scripture. It comes down as a story people have loved, told to point at something. And what does it point at? Not that prayer gets you out of work. Isidore still plows. It points at the old worry he had to face: that time given to God is time stolen from the job. In the legend the field doesn't suffer. The work gets done. There's a line in the Psalms, in the Douay-Rheims, that fits a farm as well as a building site: "Unless the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it." The farmer's version would be: unless the Lord plows the field. Isidore's story takes that literally, with oxen. Other stories told about him lean the same way. Tradition says he poured out grain for hungry birds in winter, and that his sack was still full when he reached the mill. Catholics have made him a patron of farmers and of the people who grow what everyone else eats, often without anyone noticing. In the end it's a story about a hired hand who believed the God he prayed to was also out in the field.
screen: `A HIRED HAND WHO PLOWED.` · `A LEGEND POINTING AT SOMETHING TRUE.` · `UNLESS THE LORD BUILD THE HOUSE.` · `PATRON OF THOSE WHO GROW OUR FOOD.` · then, large: `ANGELS PLOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the people who grow your food. Settle, and breathe. Think back to your last meal. Choose one thing on the plate and follow it backward. A truck. A packing shed. A field. Someone bending in the heat, or up before dawn, or worried about rain. You'll never know their name. Hold them anyway. If you pray, you can ask Saint Isidore to pray for farmers and farmworkers today. If you don't, simply let them be seen by you for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Isidore, the farmer of Madrid. A hired hand who prayed before he plowed, and whose field, legend says, angels helped to plow.
Your line: angels plow. Today, before you start your work, take one breath and give it away first. Then eat one bite slowly, and think of the field it came from. Day nine hundred ninety.

991.title: Dymphna (15 May)
991.hook: a young Irish princess of legend, patron of those with mental illness
991.howItsDone: Catholics ask Saint Dymphna's prayers for people living with anxiety, depression and other mental illness; her feast is kept on 15 May in some places, and some hospitals and ministries carry her name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isidore the Farmer, the hired hand whose field, legend says, the angels helped to plow. Your line was angels plow. Which bite did you eat slowly? Day nine hundred ninety-one.

Some saints come to us with letters and records. This one comes to us almost entirely as a story. A king's daughter in Ireland. Her mother dies, and her father's grief turns into something dark and wrong. The girl runs. With an old priest, she crosses the sea and hides in a small town in what is now Belgium. Her father follows. The story ends badly, and quickly. But that's not where the story stops. Something grows up around her grave. Today, the patron of the troubled mind. Dymphna.
screen: `A KING'S DAUGHTER.` → `SHE RUNS, ACROSS THE SEA.` → `SOMETHING GROWS AROUND HER GRAVE.`

segments.voice: Dymphna comes to us as a legend, and historians can't confirm much of it. The Church keeps her as a saint of tradition. In the legend, she flees with a priest named Gerebernus to Geel. Her father finds them there, and both are killed. Tradition says that people suffering in mind began coming to pray at her shrine, and kept coming. And here's what grew. The town did not send them away. The families of Geel began taking them in, as boarders, living in their homes, eating at their tables. Not locked away. Living alongside. The custom lasted, and Geel is still known for it. So a girl who ran from a household that had gone wrong became the patron of people whose own minds feel like a house gone wrong. Catholics turn to Dymphna for anxiety, depression, and illnesses of the mind, for themselves and for people they love. Her story doesn't promise a quick cure. It offers company, the kind Jesus promises in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "Come to me, all you that labour, and are burdened, and I will refresh you." Some Catholics pray to her alongside doctors and medicine, not instead of them. The legend is dark. What it left behind is a town that opened its doors.
screen: `A SAINT KNOWN MOSTLY BY STORY.` · `SHE FLEES TO GEEL.` · `A TOWN THAT TOOK PEOPLE IN.` · `COMPANY, ALONGSIDE CARE.` · then, large: `I WILL REFRESH YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone who is struggling in their mind. Settle, and breathe. Bring one person to mind. Someone anxious, or low, or exhausted inside. Maybe someone you love. Maybe it's you. Don't try to fix anything. Just keep them company, the way the families of Geel did. If you pray, you can ask Saint Dymphna to pray for them. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with kindness. And if you're the one struggling right now, let today include reaching out to someone you trust, or to a doctor. The bell holds the time.
Dymphna. The young princess of Irish legend who fled to Geel, honored as patron of people who suffer in mind.
Your line: for the troubled mind. Today, send one message to someone who might be having a hard time. No advice, just company. Day nine hundred ninety-one.

992.title: Brendan the Navigator (16 May)
992.hook: an Irish monk whose ocean voyage became a legend
992.howItsDone: Saint Brendan's day is kept on 16 May, especially in Ireland; Catholics remember him with prayers for sailors and travelers, and some coastal communities bless boats.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dymphna, the princess of legend and the town of Geel that opened its doors. Your line was for the troubled mind. Who did you keep company? Day nine hundred ninety-two.

A small boat of wood and hides, pushed off a rocky Irish shore. Monks at the oars, an abbot at the front, and no map for where they're going. They're looking for a land promised to the saints, somewhere out to the west. Some days the wind takes them. Some days they row. Some days they simply pull in the oars and let God steer. Then they land on a dark, bare island, light a fire to cook, and the island starts to move. Today, the monk who went out on the ocean. Brendan the Navigator.
screen: `A BOAT OF WOOD AND HIDES.` → `LOOKING FOR A PROMISED LAND.` → `THE ISLAND MOVES.`

segments.voice: There was a real Brendan, an Irish abbot who founded monasteries and is remembered as a traveler. And there is the Brendan of the Voyage, a Latin tale called the Navigatio. The two overlap, but the Voyage is a legend, and it wears its wonders openly. The moving island is a great fish. In the tale, the monks come back to it each Easter to keep the feast on its back. They find an island of birds that sing the hours of prayer. They meet a monk who has lived alone on a rock. They sail past wonders and terrors. Some readers have wondered whether a real voyage lies under the story, maybe even across the whole Atlantic, and people have argued about it. The tale itself doesn't care to prove anything. It's after something else. Irish tradition speaks of leaving home for God's sake, going out with no plan to come back; some call it a kind of white martyrdom. Brendan's boat is that idea, set afloat. The sea is huge and the boat is tiny, and the monks keep their prayers anyway, at their hours, even on the back of a whale. There's a psalm about sailors, in the Douay-Rheims: "They that go down to the sea in ships, doing business in the great waters: These have seen the works of the Lord, and his wonders in the deep." That's the Voyage in two lines. In the tale, the farther out the monks go, the more wonders they meet.
screen: `THE ABBOT, AND THE LEGEND.` · `EASTER ON THE BACK OF A WHALE.` · `LEAVING HOME FOR GOD'S SAKE.` · `PRAYERS KEPT ON A TINY BOAT.` · then, large: `HIS WONDERS IN THE DEEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the people at sea. Settle, and breathe. Let your breath come in and go out like a slow swell. Bring to mind the people out on the water right now. Fishing crews. Sailors on cargo ships, far from home for months. People crossing water in boats that aren't safe, hoping to land somewhere. Rescue crews heading out into the weather. If you pray, you can ask Saint Brendan to pray for them. If you don't, simply hold them, one boat at a time. The bell holds the time.
Navigatio, the Latin tale of Brendan the Navigator's legendary ocean voyage, carrying monks and their prayers far out to sea.
Your line: out on the ocean. Today, keep one small habit of prayer or quiet in an unfamiliar place, the way the monks did on the boat. Day nine hundred ninety-two.

993.title: Bernardine of Siena (20 May)
993.hook: a preacher who spread the letters IHS as a sign of the Holy Name
993.howItsDone: Catholics remember Saint Bernardine of Siena on 20 May; the IHS monogram he promoted appears on hosts, vestments and church buildings, and the Church keeps a memorial of the Most Holy Name of Jesus on 3 January.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Brendan the Navigator, the monks keeping their prayers on a tiny boat. Your line was out on the ocean. Where did you keep a small habit somewhere unfamiliar? Day nine hundred ninety-three.

Three letters. I, H, S. You may have seen them stamped on a communion wafer, stitched on a vestment, carved over a church door, cut into an old gravestone. Often with rays of light around them, like a sun. It is easy to walk past them without asking what they say. In the Italian towns, tradition says, a Franciscan preacher used to hold them up in front of the crowd on a painted board, gold on blue, and ask everyone to look. Today, the man with the board. Bernardine of Siena.
screen: `I, H, S.` → `ON WAFERS, DOORS, GRAVESTONES.` → `A PREACHER HOLDS UP A BOARD.`

segments.voice: First, the letters. IHS is the name Jesus, shortened, from the way it was written in Greek capitals: the first three letters of the name. Later, people read other meanings into it, Latin phrases that happen to fit the letters. Those are pious readings added afterward; the root is simply the name. Bernardine was a Franciscan friar and a preacher who traveled from town to town. Tradition says crowds came to hear him in the city squares, and that he preached against feuds and gambling and the hatreds that split towns into factions. Then he'd lift up the board with the three letters and invite people to honor the name of Jesus. Some townspeople, tradition says, burned their gaming boards and painted the letters over their own doors. Not everyone loved this. Some critics accused him of something close to idolatry, as if he were asking people to worship a painted sign. Tradition says he was examined and cleared. His answer, in effect, was that the board wasn't the point. The name was. Paul's letter puts it this way, in the Douay-Rheims: "That in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those that are in heaven, on earth, and under the earth." For Bernardine, the name was a short way to pray. Not a long speech. One word, said with love. Catholics later kept a feast of the Holy Name of Jesus, and the letters he carried spread far beyond the towns where he preached.
screen: `THE LETTERS ARE THE NAME, SHORTENED.` · `A FRIAR PREACHING IN THE SQUARES.` · `ACCUSED, EXAMINED, CLEARED.` · `ONE WORD, SAID WITH LOVE.` · then, large: `IN THE NAME OF JESUS EVERY KNEE SHOULD BOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write the name. Settle, and breathe. If you have paper, or a fogged mirror, or a note on your phone, write the three letters: I, H, S. Look at them. If you pray, you can say the name they stand for, slowly, once with each breath, and nothing else. If you don't, simply look at the letters and let them be what they are: a name, shortened, that people have carved into wood and stone. Keep your eyes on them. The bell holds the time.
IHS, the three letters of the name Jesus that Bernardine of Siena, a Franciscan preacher, held up so crowds would honor the holy name.
Your line: the holy name. Today, look for those three letters, in a church, on a gravestone, in a picture. And notice how you say other people's names. Day nine hundred ninety-three.

994.title: The Mexican martyrs (21 May)
994.hook: Christopher Magallanes and companions killed during the Cristero years
994.howItsDone: On 21 May the Church keeps an optional memorial of Saint Christopher Magallanes and companions; in Mexico, Catholics often pray for their country and visit shrines connected to the martyrs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bernardine of Siena and his board with three letters. Your line was the holy name. Where did you spot IHS? Day nine hundred ninety-four.

¡Viva Cristo Rey! Long live Christ the King. In Mexico, in the years of the Cristero conflict, those words could be a battle cry, a password, a prayer, or the last thing someone said. This week we've met an apostle who asked to see the Father, a replacement chosen by lot, a farmer, a princess of legend, a sailor monk and a preacher with a painted board. Today the week ends in a country where calling Christ king could cost you your life. Today, the Mexican martyrs.
screen: `¡VIVA CRISTO REY!` → `A CRY, A PRAYER, LAST WORDS.` → `THE WEEK ENDS IN MEXICO.`

segments.voice: Some background, kept simple. There was a time when Mexico's government passed harsh laws limiting the Church: priests registered and restricted, schools and orders closed. In protest, the bishops suspended public Masses across the country. Some Catholics took up arms, and the fighters came to be called Cristeros. It was a real war, with violence on more than one side, and the Church doesn't canonize a war. What the Church honors on this day is different. It honors Christopher Magallanes, a parish priest, and a group of companions, priests among them, who were killed for their faith during those years. Tradition remembers Father Magallanes as a pastor who ran a seminary in secret, cared for his people, and did not urge them to take up arms. When he was arrested and brought to be shot, the story goes, he gave away what he had and said he was innocent and forgave those who were about to kill him. Some of the martyrs, tradition says, died with that cry on their lips: Viva Cristo Rey. Here is the line under the whole day. Jesus, in the Douay-Rheims: "Love your enemies: do good to them that hate you: and pray for them that persecute and calumniate you." That's the strange part of these martyrs. Their cry sounds like a battle shout. But the ones the Church remembers here are honored for dying without hatred. Long live Christ the King, said by a man forgiving the soldiers in front of him. A king, in this faith, who was crowned with thorns.
screen: `HARSH LAWS, AND A WAR.` · `A PRIEST WHO DIDN'T TAKE UP ARMS.` · `HE FORGAVE HIS KILLERS.` · `A CRY SAID WITHOUT HATRED.` · then, large: `LOVE YOUR ENEMIES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold Mexico. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the country as it is today. Its cities and villages. Its families, its parishes, its priests. People living with violence, and people working for peace. Those who have gone north and those waiting at home. If you pray, you can ask the Mexican martyrs to pray for Mexico, or simply say their cry quietly: long live Christ the King. If you don't, hold the people of Mexico in mind, with goodwill, one face at a time. The bell holds the time.
Christopher Magallanes, the priest remembered with his companions as the Mexican martyrs, killed in the Cristero years, honored for dying without hatred.
Your line: long live christ the king. Today, when someone wrongs you, try answering without hatred, even once. Day nine hundred ninety-four.

options: lead them into battle.
keep serving your people in secret.

fork.reveal: tradition remembers Magallanes running a seminary in secret and caring for his people. he was killed anyway, forgiving his executioners.
